notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Moses while the Israelites were camped near Mount Sinai. These instructions were given before the people packed up to march toward Canaan. They established how Israel was to manage the land once they settled in their new home.

God told Moses that when the Israelites entered the Promised Land, the ground itself had to observe a Sabbath rest to the Lord. Just as people rested on the seventh day of the week, the farmland was to rest every seventh year. This reminded Israel that the land was a gift from God and belonged to Him.

The Israelites were allowed to plant crops and prune grapevines for six straight years. They could do all normal farm work and gather their grain and fruit during that time. God honored their hard work, but placed it within a repeating seven-year cycle.

In the seventh year, the land was given complete rest dedicated to the Lord. The people were forbidden from planting fields, pruning vineyards, or harvesting any crops that sprouted on their own. Leaving the ground alone showed deep trust that God would provide without their daily labor.

Whatever grew naturally in the fields during the Sabbath year served as food for everyone. Landowners, servants, day laborers, resident foreigners, domestic animals, and wild beasts all shared the food equally. No one was allowed to hoard the crops or store them in barns for private profit.

Israel was instructed to count seven cycles of seven years, which added up to forty-nine years. Each of these seven-year blocks ended with a Sabbath year of rest for the soil. Tracking these cycles built anticipation for a grand celebration that followed.

At the end of forty-nine years, a ram's horn was sounded across the entire country on the Day of Atonement. This was the annual day when God cleansed the sins of the nation and reconciled the people to Himself. Proclaiming national freedom on this exact day showed that human forgiveness flows out of God's forgiveness.

The fiftieth year was set apart as a sacred Year of Jubilee, when liberty was proclaimed across the land. Enslaved Hebrews were set free, and families who had sold property received their ancestral land back. This kept the original tribal lands intact and prevented poor families from being ruined forever.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholarship notes that the Jubilee's release applied to Israelite servants rather than foreign slaves, meaning it was not a complete abolition of all slavery.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching views the Jubilee's call to cancel debts and restore land as a biblical model for economic justice, such as relieving the debts of poor nations.

notes.meaning: The fiftieth year was a holy Jubilee, so farming was halted just as it was in a Sabbath year. The people were not to sow seeds, prune vines, or gather crops into storage houses. Instead, they ate only what grew on its own, picking it directly from the field day by day.

In this Jubilee year, every person returned to the piece of land originally given to their ancestors. No matter why a family had lost or transferred its property, the ground came back to them. This system protected families from falling into permanent poverty.

Whenever Israelites bought or sold property to a neighbor, they were commanded not to cheat or take advantage of one another. Buyers were not to exploit a poor neighbor's desperation, and sellers could not demand more than fair market value. God required strict honesty in every financial agreement.

The sale price of land was calculated by counting the number of harvest years left until the next Jubilee. If many years remained, the price was high, but if the Jubilee was near, the price was low. The buyer was not purchasing the permanent dirt, but only the right to harvest crops until the land returned home.

God repeats His warning against mistreating neighbors and connects fair business to the fear of the Lord. Honoring God means treating others with justice and compassion, especially in money matters. God sees every deal and holds people accountable when they wrong someone else.

God promised that faithful obedience to His laws would bring safety and abundance in the land. The soil would produce generous crops so the people could eat until they were full. True peace and security came from trusting God rather than relying on military strength.

God anticipated that the Israelites would worry about what they would eat during the seventh year. Since they were forbidden to sow or harvest, running out of food was a natural human fear. God voiced their unspoken concern so He could comfort them with His promise.

God promised to send a special blessing in the sixth year, making the land produce enough food to last for three full years. Israel would live off this stored grain through the seventh year of rest and the eighth year of planting, until the new harvest arrived in the ninth year. This miracle demonstrated God's supernatural power to care for those who obey Him.

The land could never be sold permanently because God owned it outright. The Israelites lived there as His tenants and resident guests under His covenant care. Because the property belonged to God alone, no family could permanently lose their inheritance.

In every sale of land, Israel was required to allow for its redemption. To redeem something means to buy it back and restore it to its rightful place. No contract was valid if it prevented a poor family from reclaiming their property before the Jubilee.

If an Israelite became poor and was forced to sell family land, his nearest relative had the right to step forward and buy it back. This relative, called a redeemer, protected the family name and inheritance. Many Christians see this kinsman redeemer as a picture of Jesus, who took on human flesh to buy back our lost inheritance.

If a poor man had no relative to help him, but later gained enough wealth, he could buy the land back himself. He calculated how many years had passed since the sale and paid the buyer the balance for the remaining years until the Jubilee. Once that fair refund was paid, he took back his ancestral home without delay.

If the seller could not afford to buy back his field, the buyer kept possession of it until the Year of Jubilee. When that fiftieth year arrived, the property was freely handed back to the original owner with no money required. This guaranteed that every family regained their home through God's gracious law.
